title: Knowledge check: Structure of an HTTP Request

questions.prompt: When investigating an HTTP interaction, which inspection sequence is most reliable?
options: Treat a browser URL fragment as part of the HTTP request target.
Assume DNS, TLS, and application routing are the same layer.
Inspect the method and target, request headers/body, response status, response headers, and response body.
Inspect only the JSON body and ignore the method and status.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the method and target, request headers/body, response status, response headers, and response body.
questions.explanation: Inspect the method and target, request headers/body, response status, response headers, and response body. This is especially relevant to “Structure of an HTTP Request” because the API contract must remain explicit and reviewable.

questions.prompt: For the lesson “Structure of an HTTP Request”, which check provides the strongest practical evidence?
options: Test against production records so the exercise cannot be repeated safely.
Compare the complete HTTP message with the target URL structure and transport evidence.
Rely on a code review comment without running any representative check.
Run one happy-path call and skip invalid, denied, and failure scenarios.
questions.answer_key: Compare the complete HTTP message with the target URL structure and transport evidence.
questions.explanation: A useful check is repeatable, tied to an observable contract, and includes an important negative or boundary scenario.

questions.prompt: Which review warning is most relevant to “Structure of an HTTP Request”?
options: A diagnosis mixes network, HTTP, and application layers without inspecting the actual messages.
The expected behavior and relevant failure cases are documented.
A representative test can reproduce the result.
The API avoids exposing internal secrets and personal data.
questions.answer_key: A diagnosis mixes network, HTTP, and application layers without inspecting the actual messages.
questions.explanation: This finding weakens a core API guarantee and should be treated as a design or release issue, not only a style concern.
